Key Takeaways

Options markets imply Walmart shares could move about 6% either way after earnings later this week.

Analysts expect Walmart to report $187.3 billion in revenue and $5.02 billion in net income.

Walmart's stock has risen for months. Could this week's earnings report extend that?

We'll find out soon. The retail giant is set to turn in its third-quarter results Thursday morning, one of the last big reports of the current earnings season, with Wall Street analysts looking for revenue of $187.3 billion and net income of $5.02 billion according to Visible Alpha. The numbers are due with the stock up 15% this year—and slightly outperforming the S&P 500—after a climb off early-autumn lows.

Investors expect Walmart (WMT) shares to move substantially in the coming days. Based on Investopedia's calculation using Monday's closing price and recent options market data, the stock is seen moving about 6% in either direction by the end of the week. That could mean a rise to near $136, or a retreat to about $121.

Walmart's shares came under pressure after its midyear report included a less-optimistic third-quarter revenue and EPS outlook than investors expected.

Wall Street's current outlook for the shares is on the tepid side. Visible Alpha's mean price target for the stock is around $130, just slightly above yesterday's finish.

Investors also watch Walmart's numbers and executive commentary for clues about the direction of the U.S. economy and the health of the American consumer. The Census Bureau early Tuesday said U.S. retail sales rose 0.2% in October from September, in line with investors' expectations.

DoorDash (DASH) stock closed at $169.78 on November 16, 2026. That price sits 14.5% below its November 4 close, and a fall that quick tempts buyers to step in. It is not yet as deep as the 20%-plus drops below, but those show how buying after a sharp fall has played out. A 40% rally would fit the stock's own past. Within a year of earlier sharp drops, the shares at some point stood a median 49.7% above the dip-date price. Reaching a high is not the same as keeping it, however. So where did buyers stand a full year after those earlier drops?

Most DoorDash Dip Buyers Were Down A Year Later

Since December 2020, DoorDash stock has fallen more than 20% within 30 trading days eight times. Seven of those drops have a full year behind them, and the shares were higher 12 months later after only three. The median result a year on was a loss of 8.0%. The latest drop, in February 2026, remains too recent to judge.

The path after a drop was rough, too. In the year after a typical drop, the shares closed at a low a median 28.1% below the dip-date price. The best price of that year arrived a median 267 days after the drop, requiring close to nine months of holding on.

FICO, Costco, and Ford have important interim updates ahead that could offer fresh clues about consumer credit, spending, and the auto industry

Costco's special $30 dividend and upcoming sales report put the retail giant in the spotlight heading into the peak of the holiday shopping season

Ford's sales trends and TSMC's chip revenue will provide additional insights into the economy and AI investment momentum before year-end

Who knew the third week of November would be so jam-packed with volatility catalysts? NVIDIA (NVDA) earnings, the Anthropic (ANT) IPO, Trump/XI/Putin, retail sales, FOMC minutes, a slew of Fed speak, and earnings from Walmart (WMT), Target (TGT), and Home Depot (HD)... all paint the tape. U.S. traders will earn their Thanksgiving holiday break next week, with more key firm-specific data on tap later this month and in early December.

Notable interim reports are indeed on tap. Updates from Fair Isaac (FICO), Costco (COST), and Ford (F) are three our team will watch through mid-December. These early reads on consumer and business trends often lay the macro foundation further out. You can track all the crucial interim data events on our Interim Calendar. Here are the three reports and why they matter:

1. Friday, November 20: Fair Isaac Corp.

FICO is the definition of a story stock. It also underscores material changes happening in the consumer credit space. Would-be borrowers and personal finance aficionados are surely familiar with the FICO® Score, which boasted a near-monopoly in the credit-reporting niche. Individuals seeking to take out loans would first shore up their FICO® Score, then apply for funds from banks, auto companies, or other financial institutions. The three major credit bureaus were sort of in the middle, and they closely monitored applicants' creditworthiness.

That's how things used to be. Today, VantageScore disrupts FICO's dominance. It's a privately held joint venture owned by Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, but operated independently. Its VantageScore 4.0 is now permitted for eligible Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mortgages, and borrowers can view this score for free on various platforms. The FICO® Score, by contrast, was a closely guarded computation in the bygone era.

Macro context matters here. The housing market is dreadful, as evidenced by last week's 16-year low in existing home sales growth. Mortgage rates remain well north of 7%, too, which suppresses the weekly tally of new home loan applications. Still, FICO (down 57% YTD) has bounced to $720 per share from below in late September. We'll see what the fundamental monthly statement reveals on Black Friday.

Factors Likely to Have Supported WMT's Q3 Performance

Walmart's expanding omnichannel capabilities are likely to have supported quarterly performance. Higher-margin businesses, including advertising, membership and marketplace services, are expected to have contributed to profitability. Continued growth in Walmart Connect, expanding fulfillment services and membership penetration may have supported a favorable business mix. Supply-chain automation, improved delivery density and technology-driven productivity initiatives could have strengthened e-commerce economics and operational efficiency.

Walmart International and Sam's Club U.S. are also likely to have contributed to consolidated growth. Management specifically expects both businesses to remain growth-accretive during the quarter. Strength in China, expanding international digital capabilities and sustained membership engagement at Sam's Club may have supported performance.

These growth drivers underpin management's projection of third-quarter net sales growth of 3%-3.75% on a constant-currency basis.

title: The Waltons Won a Tax Court Case in 2000 That Lets a Family Pass a Stock’s Growth to Heirs While Reporting a Taxable Gift of Nearly $0. The Trust It Approved Is Still Legal
detail:
The Waltons Won a Tax Court Case in 2000 That Lets a Family Pass a Stock’s Growth to Heirs While Reporting a Taxable Gift of Nearly $0. The Trust It Approved Is Still Legal
Vilma Rios

WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase

Quick Read

Walmart heir Audrey Walton beat the IRS in 2000, when a unanimous Tax Court struck down its reading of Example 5 as invalid.

A widow moving $2 million of stock into a two-year GRAT reports a taxable gift of about $1 while passing roughly $514,000 of growth to her children.

Holding the stock instead would cost heirs about $205,000 in estate tax, though a GRAT leaves children her original basis with no step-up.

Many financial professionals are salespeople paid on what they push, not whether you end up wealthier. A fiduciary is the opposite. The SEC legally requires them to put your interests first. Advisor.com's free matching tool pairs you with vetted fiduciaries from major national firms, all in under three minutes. See who you match with today.

A 68-year-old widow owns $2 million of a single growth stock, part of an estate worth about $20 million. That puts her above the 2026 basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000. Any gain the stock makes from here lands in an estate that is already over the line.

Mlenny / Getty Images

Her attorney sets up a two-year trust. She moves the stock in and holds the right to two annual payments of $1,075,609. Her Form 709 reports a taxable gift of about $1.41. If the stock gains 20% a year, her children end the two years owning $513,660 of it outright, and none of that growth ever counts against her exemption.

The structure is a grantor retained annuity trust, or GRAT. The version she used exists today because a Walmart heir took the IRS to court and won.

How Audrey Walton Beat the IRS With Walmart Stock

Audrey J. Walton held more than seven million shares of Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT). In 1993 she put about 3.6 million shares into each of two GRATs. Each trust was worth just over $100 million and paid her 49.35% of its starting value in year one and 59.22% in year two. If she died during the term, the payments went to her estate. One daughter was the remainder beneficiary of each trust.

She reported each gift at $0. The IRS relied on Treasury Regulation 25.2702-3(e), Example 5, and argued that her chance of dying during the term reduced her retained interest. On that theory each gift was worth $3,821,522.12, and the agency assessed a deficiency of $4,532,776.82. Valued as a plain two-year annuity, each gift came to $6,195.10.

The recommendations of Wall Street analysts are often relied on by investors when deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock. Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though?

Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Walmart (WMT).

Walmart currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.35, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 41 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.35 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 41 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 30 are Strong Buy and seven are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 73.2% and 17.1% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for WMT
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for WMT

Check price target & stock forecast for Walmart here>>>

The ABR suggests buying Walmart, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.

This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.

Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR

Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether.

The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.
